title: Machines at Work
text:
Automation is reshaping the labour market at a pace that many economists find difficult to predict. Routine tasks in manufacturing and data entry have already been delegated to machines, while the demand for workers who can interpret results and make judgements has grown. Such shifts, however, do not necessarily translate into mass unemployment. Historically, technological change has tended to create new occupations even as it eliminates old ones.

The real challenge, therefore, lies less in the number of jobs than in their quality and distribution. Workers displaced from declining sectors often lack the training needed to move into emerging fields, which can deepen regional and social divides. Many analysts argue that continuous retraining programmes, funded collaboratively by governments and employers, are essential to ensure that the benefits of innovation are shared broadly.

questions.text: According to the passage, what has already been delegated to machines?
options: Routine tasks in manufacturing and data entry

questions.text: What do workers displaced from declining sectors often lack?
options: The training needed for emerging fields

questions.text: What does the author imply about the effect of technology on total employment?
options: It has no effect on the occupations available.
It may remove old jobs while creating new ones.
It only benefits workers with advanced degrees.

questions.text: Why does the author suggest that retraining programmes are important?
options: They are mainly needed in manufacturing.
They would reduce the number of jobs available.
They would ensure the gains of innovation are widely shared.

paragraph_translations: La automatización está transformando el mercado laboral a un ritmo que muchos economistas encuentran difícil de predecir. Las tareas rutinarias en la manufactura y la introducción de datos ya han sido delegadas a las máquinas, mientras que ha crecido la demanda de trabajadores capaces de interpretar resultados y emitir juicios. Sin embargo, estos cambios no se traducen necesariamente en desempleo masivo. Históricamente, el cambio tecnológico ha tendido a crear nuevas ocupaciones aun cuando elimina las antiguas.

El verdadero desafío, por tanto, reside menos en la cantidad de empleos que en su calidad y distribución. Los trabajadores desplazados de sectores en declive suelen carecer de la formación necesaria para incorporarse a campos emergentes, lo que puede profundizar las brechas regionales y sociales. Muchos analistas sostienen que los programas continuos de reciclaje profesional, financiados de manera conjunta por gobiernos y empleadores, son esenciales para que los beneficios de la innovación se compartan ampliamente.
